title: AI Feedback on Drafts

prompt.professorQuestion: Over the past year, many instructors have debated whether to permit artificial intelligence writing assistants in university courses. Some argue that students should be allowed to use AI tools for instant feedback on preliminary drafts, while others believe that such tools should be strictly restricted to protect independent critical thinking. What is your position on this issue? Whose argument do you find more compelling?

studentOpinions.stance: I strongly support allowing AI feedback on early drafts. Students often study late at night when writing tutors are unavailable. Getting immediate suggestions on grammar and sentence clarity helps learners refine their work before class.
studentOpinions.opinion: I strongly support allowing AI feedback on early drafts. Students often study late at night when writing tutors are unavailable. Getting immediate suggestions on grammar and sentence clarity helps learners refine their work before class.

studentOpinions.stance: I think we should restrict these tools. When students rely too much on automated feedback, they simply accept algorithmic changes without thinking critically about why their original sentences needed improvement.
studentOpinions.opinion: I think we should restrict these tools. When students rely too much on automated feedback, they simply accept algorithmic changes without thinking critically about why their original sentences needed improvement.

modelEssay:
While I understand Sarah’s concern that students might passively accept computer suggestions, I agree with Michael that AI feedback on early drafts can be a valuable learning aid when used responsibly.

In my view, AI assistants should function as digital sounding boards rather than ghostwriters. For instance, in my introductory sociology class, I frequently used an AI tool to check whether my thesis statement was logically connected to my topic sentences. Instead of letting the software rewrite my paragraphs, I used its feedback to identify weak transitions and rethink my explanations. This allowed my professor to focus on evaluating my analytical arguments during office hours rather than correcting basic grammatical errors. As long as instructors require students to reflect on the revisions they make, AI tools will foster greater academic independence.

title: Recorded Lectures or Live Attendance

Should universities record every lecture and make videos available online, or should institutions emphasize mandatory in-person attendance? Which approach is more beneficial for student learning?

studentOpinions.opinion: Recording every lecture is essential. Complex explanations in science or math often require multiple viewings. If students can pause and review difficult concepts at their own pace, comprehension increases significantly.

modelEssay:
Although Sarah makes a valid point about the value of spontaneous classroom interaction, I find Michael's argument in favor of recording lectures much more compelling.

Having access to recorded lectures is particularly crucial for mastering rigorous, cumulative subjects. For example, during my organic chemistry course, the professor introduced dozens of complex reaction mechanisms during each fifty-minute class. Being able to rewatch tricky fifteen-minute segments allowed me to take thorough notes and clarify confusing steps before the next lab session. Furthermore, lecture captures provide an indispensable safety net for working students or commuters who occasionally face transit delays. Rather than discouraging attendance, recorded videos reduce academic anxiety and allow students to engage more deeply with challenging course material.

modelEssay:

Translation software is best used as a vocabulary bridge rather than a total crutch. For instance, when analyzing complex philosophical treatises, an international student can quickly look up specialized terminologies in their native tongue to grasp the theoretical framework, and then formulate their written arguments in English. This targeted approach prevents cognitive overload and boosts students' confidence. Ultimately, intelligent use of translation software accelerates conceptual understanding without sacrificing English development.

An automated notification sent to an academic advisor can trigger a supportive check-in, offering tutoring resources before midterm grades drop. When universities use student data transparently for academic support rather than punitive evaluation, digital tracking becomes an empowering safety net rather than an intrusive monitor.

title: Campus Facial Recognition

prompt.professorQuestion: Several universities are testing facial recognition scanners at dormitory entrances and laboratory facilities to enhance security. Do you support adopting biometric facial scans on campus, or should universities stick to traditional plastic ID keycards?

studentOpinions.stance: Facial recognition is extremely convenient and safe. Students frequently lose plastic keycards or lend them to outsiders. Face scans guarantee that only authorized residents enter residence halls.
studentOpinions.opinion: Facial recognition is extremely convenient and safe. Students frequently lose plastic keycards or lend them to outsiders. Face scans guarantee that only authorized residents enter residence halls.

studentOpinions.stance: Biometric scanning goes too far. Storing facial data creates immense cybersecurity risks if campus servers are hacked, and it normalizes invasive surveillance in students' living spaces.
studentOpinions.opinion: Biometric scanning goes too far. Storing facial data creates immense cybersecurity risks if campus servers are hacked, and it normalizes invasive surveillance in students' living spaces.

modelEssay:
While Michael highlights the practical convenience of keyless entry, I strongly side with Sarah in opposing facial recognition systems across university campuses.

Biometric data is fundamentally different from a plastic access badge because if a database is compromised, students cannot change their facial patterns like a lost password. High-profile data breaches occur regularly at universities, making centralized biometric databases attractive targets for cybercriminals. Furthermore, facial recognition software has documented error rates that disproportionately misidentify minority students, causing unwarranted access denials. Traditional magnetic keycards paired with two-factor authentication or mobile phone credentials offer excellent security without subjecting students to constant surveillance in their private residence halls. Protecting student privacy and digital rights must take precedence over minor daily conveniences.

Moreover, glancing at a phone sends a disrespectful message to peers presenting their ideas. Instead of relying on handheld devices, instructors can encourage students to use laptops dedicated solely to note-taking or provide brief pauses for factual lookups. Establishing phone-free zones during discussions protects cognitive focus and fosters a more collaborative, respectful classroom atmosphere.

Planting shade trees today is a permanent, cost-effective investment that heals urban ecology and enriches public health for future generations.

title: Quiet Spaces at Work

prompt.professorQuestion: Modern open-plan offices generate constant noise, ringing phones, and visual interruptions. Should corporate employers designate dedicated soundproof 'quiet wellness rooms' where employees can meditate, pray, or sit silently without screens, or should employers prioritize managing workload expectations directly?

studentOpinions.stance: Quiet rooms provide immediate neurological relief. A quiet ten-minute break from sensory overload calms heart rates, lowers cortisol, and restores cognitive sharpness.
studentOpinions.opinion: Quiet rooms provide immediate neurological relief. A quiet ten-minute break from sensory overload calms heart rates, lowers cortisol, and restores cognitive sharpness.

studentOpinions.stance: Quiet rooms are superficial band-aids. If workers are overwhelmed by sixty-hour workloads and unachievable deadlines, sitting silently in a dark room does nothing to cure workplace stress.
studentOpinions.opinion: Quiet rooms are superficial band-aids. If workers are overwhelmed by sixty-hour workloads and unachievable deadlines, sitting silently in a dark room does nothing to cure workplace stress.

modelEssay:
While Sarah is completely right that quiet rooms cannot fix systemic overwork and exploitative corporate deadlines, I side with Michael that establishing dedicated soundproof quiet sanctuaries is an essential workplace wellness requirement.

Open-plan office environments expose workers to chronic acoustic overstimulation: overheard sales calls, clattering keyboards, and footsteps keep nervous systems in perpetual high alert. Even employees with reasonable workloads experience acute cognitive fatigue from constant interruptions. A screen-free quiet room offers a sanctuary where employees can practice deep breathing, conduct daily prayers, or decompress in tranquil silence. Neuroscientific research confirms that taking a ten-minute sensory respite down-regulates sympathetic nervous stress, relieves tension headaches, and enhances mental clarity upon returning to one's desk. Providing quiet rooms is an affordable, compassionate environmental accommodation that protects employee mental hygiene.

title: Nutrition Classes for Children

prompt.professorQuestion: Children consume unprecedented amounts of ultra-processed packaged snacks. Should primary schools incorporate mandatory hands-on culinary nutrition and cooking classes into the weekly curriculum, or should instructional time be reserved strictly for core academic subjects like mathematics and reading?

studentOpinions.stance: Cooking is a vital survival skill. Teaching kids to prepare fresh vegetables, read food labels, and cook basic meals empowers them to make healthy food choices for the rest of their lives.
studentOpinions.opinion: Cooking is a vital survival skill. Teaching kids to prepare fresh vegetables, read food labels, and cook basic meals empowers them to make healthy food choices for the rest of their lives.

studentOpinions.stance: Curriculum schedules are already strained. Schools must prioritize reading and math proficiency; cooking and nutrition are parental responsibilities best learned at home.
studentOpinions.opinion: Curriculum schedules are already strained. Schools must prioritize reading and math proficiency; cooking and nutrition are parental responsibilities best learned at home.

modelEssay:
Although Sarah reasonably emphasizes that schools must maintain high standards in foundational reading and mathematics literacy, I strongly agree with Michael that teaching hands-on culinary nutrition in primary schools is an indispensable life skill.

Relying on parents to teach cooking overlooks modern economic realities: millions of time-crunched working parents lack cooking skills themselves and rely entirely on packaged convenience foods. When schools treat nutrition as an irrelevant extracurricular hobby, children grow up dependent on sugary fast food, paving the way for chronic adult illnesses. In contrast, teaching children to peel carrots, assemble colorful salads, and understand ingredient labels demystifies fresh food and instills pride in culinary creation. Integrating cooking also reinforces academic concepts: measuring flour teaches fractions, and studying baking chemical reactions teaches practical science. Culinary nutrition classes cultivate self-reliance and build a lifelong foundation of vibrant personal wellness.
